block/plain: A plain layer replaces its input with something new. A residual block keeps its input, x, and adds a change to it.
block/add: The layers inside, a conv, a ReLU and another conv, compute F of x. A shortcut carries x around them, and the two are added: y equals x plus F of x.
block/example: If x is two, minus one and three, and F gives a half, a half and minus one, then y is two and a half, minus a half, and two.
block/zero: To leave its input alone, a block only has to make F zero. So an extra block need not make the network worse.
block/match: The sum needs x and F of x in the same shape. When F shrinks the size with a stride, or changes the channels, the shortcut becomes a one by one conv with that stride, to match.
gradient/split: Going backward, the sum is an add gate: it hands the gradient arriving at y, g, to both of its inputs.
gradient/paths: Along the shortcut, g reaches x unchanged. Through F, it gets multiplied by F's slope, F prime.
gradient/formula: The two paths add up at x: g times one plus F prime. With g equal to two and a slope of a half, that is three.
gradient/deep: Now stack fifty layers. If each one halves the gradient, almost nothing reaches the first. With shortcuts, each block multiplies by one plus a slope, so the gradient arrives intact.
